lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Scrollwork and twists are the decorative heart of ornamental ironwork. In Africa, from the wrought-iron gates of Marrakech to the balconies of Cape Town, these elements turn plain metal into art that sells. As a self-taught blacksmith, you can charge 30-50% more for a gate with scrolls than a plain one. A simple twist on a burglar bar can make it a feature rather than a cage.

Why does it matter for your business? Because customers want identity. A scroll pattern can mimic traditional motifsâlike the Adinkra symbols of Ghana or Ndebele geometric patternsâmaking your work culturally relevant. Twists add strength and visual rhythm. A 12mm square bar twisted 3 times per 300mm is both structural and beautiful.

You don't need expensive machines. A forge, an anvil, a vice, a hammer, and a scroll jig (which you can make from scrap) are enough. Start with mild steelâit's cheap and forgiving. Practice on 8mm round bar: heat to cherry red (about 900Â°C), bend around a jig, and quench in oil to set. One hour of practice per day for a week and you'll have your first sellable scroll.

In this module, you'll learn to make consistent scrolls and twists, avoid common breaks, and work safely. By the end, you'll produce a small decorative panel that you can show to clients. Remember: in Africa's growing construction market, decorative ironwork is in demand for homes, lodges, and offices. Master these skills and you control your income.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body:
To do scrollwork and twists, you need the right tools. Start with a forgeâa simple charcoal or gas forge works. Charcoal is cheap in most African markets; a bag costs about $5 and lasts a week. For gas, a 9kg cylinder and a burner kit will set you back $150 but gives cleaner heat. You also need an anvil (any heavy steel block works; a 50kg piece of railway line is perfect), a cross-peen hammer (1-2kg), a flat hammer, and a wire brush.

For scrolls, make or buy a scroll jig. You can weld three pieces of 20mm round bar onto a base plate: one center pin and two outer pins to guide the curve. For twists, a sturdy vice and a twisting wrench (a long pipe wrench or a custom-made fork) are essential. You'll also need a hacksaw, angle grinder with cutting and grinding discs, and a set of files.

Materials: mild steel is your best friend. Use 8mm, 10mm, or 12mm round or square bar. Square bar twists more crisply; round bar scrolls smoother. Buy from local scrap yards or steel merchantsâprices vary, but expect $1-2 per meter for 10mm round. Avoid high-carbon steel (like old files) for scrolls; it cracks when bent cold. For twists, mild steel is fine.

Safety gear: leather gloves, safety glasses, earplugs, and a leather apron. In Africa's heat, wear cotton clothing, not synthetic. Keep a bucket of water and a first-aid kit nearby. A fire extinguisher is a must if using gas. With these tools, you're ready to start.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body:
Step 1: Design your scroll. Draw it on paper or directly on the floor with chalk. A classic scroll is a spiral that starts tight and opens up. For a 200mm scroll, start with a 300mm length of 10mm round bar. Mark the center.

Step 2: Heat the bar. Place it in the forge until it's cherry red (about 900Â°C). Don't let it sparkleâthat's too hot and burns the steel. Hold it with tongs.

Step 3: Form the eye. With the hot bar, hammer a small 180Â° bend at one end around a 20mm pin on your jig. This is the 'eye' of the scroll. Work quickly; you have about 30 seconds before it cools.

Step 4: Scroll the spiral. Place the eye over the center pin of your jig. Pull the bar around the pin, using the outer pins as guides. Apply steady pressureâdon't jerk. If it cools, reheat. For a tight scroll, use a smaller center pin (15mm); for an open scroll, use 25mm.

Step 5: Twist a bar. For a twist, heat a 300mm section of 10mm square bar to cherry red. Clamp one end in a vice. Attach your twisting wrench to the other end. Turn it clockwise 3 full turns for a tight twist, or 1.5 turns for a loose twist. Keep the heat even; if one part is cooler, it won't twist evenly.

Step 6: Assemble. Weld or forge-weld scrolls to a frame. For a simple panel, make a rectangular frame from 20mm square bar, then weld scrolls inside. Clean welds with a grinder, then brush and oil while warm for a black finish.

Practice each step separately before combining. With 2 hours of practice, you'll make a basic scroll. With 10 hours, you'll be consistent.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body:
Mistake 1: Overheating the steel. If you heat until it sparks, the steel burns and becomes weak. Fix: Heat only to cherry red (900Â°C). In daylight, watch for a dull red; in dark, a bright red. Use a magnetâwhen it stops sticking, it's at the right temperature.

Mistake 2: Twisting cold. Cold steel cracks when twisted. Fix: Always heat to cherry red before twisting. If you hear a crack, stop and reheat.

Mistake 3: Uneven scrolls. Your scrolls look different each time. Fix: Use a jig with fixed pins. Mark your starting point on the bar with a soapstone. Count your hammer blowsâconsistency comes from repetition.

Mistake 4: Weak welds. Welds break under load. Fix: Clean the metal to bare shine before welding. Use a 2.5mm electrode at 80-100 amps for 10mm bar. Forge-weld for stronger joints: heat both ends to welding heat (bright yellow, almost white), sprinkle borax, and hammer together.

Mistake 5: Rust. Your finished piece rusts in a month. Fix: Brush off scale with a wire brush while hot, then apply linseed oil or a metal primer. In humid African coastal areas, use a zinc-rich primer.

Mistake 6: Bending the wrong way. You twist counter-clockwise and the pattern looks off. Fix: Decide direction before you start. For a right-hand twist, turn clockwise when viewed from the end.

Mistake 7: Using the wrong steel. You grab a piece of rebar and it cracks. Fix: Rebar is often high-carbon or brittle. Stick to mild steelâtest by bending a cold piece; if it bends without cracking, it's good.

Each mistake teaches you. Keep a notebook of what works. Soon you'll avoid these entirely.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body:
Safety first. In Africa, many workshops are informal, but that's no excuse for accidents. Always wear safety glassesâhot scale flies when you hammer. Leather gloves protect from burns and cuts. Wear earplugs when grinding or hammering; hearing loss is permanent. A leather apron and closed shoes (not sandals) are a must.

Fire safety: Keep a bucket of water and a fire extinguisher near the forge. Never leave a fire unattended. If using gas, check hoses for leaks with soapy water. Store gas cylinders upright, outside the workshop. Charcoal forges produce carbon monoxideâwork in a well-ventilated area, ideally outdoors or with a chimney.

Tool safety: Before use, check hammers for loose heads. Grinders should have guards. Never use a grinder without the handle. When twisting, ensure the vice is secureâa flying bar can kill. Use a twisting wrench with a long handle to keep your hands away from the hot metal.

Best practices: Plan your work. Draw full-size templates. Keep your work area cleanâtripping over scrap causes falls. Quench hot metal in oil, not water, for mild steel to avoid cracking. For a professional finish, brush off scale and apply oil while the metal is warm (about 200Â°C).

In Africa's heat, take breaks and drink water. Heat exhaustion is real. Work in the morning or evening. If you feel dizzy, stop. Teach apprentices safety from day one. A safe workshop is a productive workshop. Your reputation depends on quality and safety.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body:
Now put it all together. Your task: make a decorative panel 300mm x 300mm with four scrolls and two twisted bars. This is a sellable itemâyou can mount it on a gate or sell as a wall piece.

Materials: 2 meters of 10mm round bar (for scrolls), 1 meter of 10mm square bar (for twists), 1.2 meters of 20mm square bar (for frame). Tools: forge, anvil, hammer, scroll jig, vice, twisting wrench, welder, angle grinder, wire brush.

Step 1: Cut the frame. Cut two 300mm pieces and two 260mm pieces of 20mm square bar. Weld into a 300x300mm square. Grind welds smooth.

Step 2: Make four scrolls. Cut four 250mm pieces of 10mm round bar. Heat and form a scroll on your jig, each with a 20mm eye. Make them as identical as possible. Quench in oil.

Step 3: Make two twisted bars. Cut two 260mm pieces of 10mm square bar. Heat the middle 200mm and twist 3 full turns clockwise. Do both the same.

Step 4: Assemble. Arrange scrolls in the corners of the frame, pointing inward. Weld them to the frame. Place the twisted bars horizontally across the center, 50mm apart. Weld.

Step 5: Finish. Heat the whole panel with a torch or in the forge to about 200Â°C (just too hot to touch). Brush with a wire brush to remove scale. Apply linseed oil or black paint. Let cool.

Step 6: Evaluate. Check that scrolls are even, twists are tight, and welds are strong. Show to a friend or potential customer. Ask for feedback. If you can make this in 3 hours, you're ready for client work. Repeat the exercise until you can do it in 2 hours. Then try a more complex design with 8 scrolls. Practice makes profit.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of adding scrollwork to a gate?
options: A) It makes the gate heavier
B) It increases the selling price
C) It reduces the need for paint
D) It makes the gate easier to weld
quiz.explanation: Decorative scrollwork can increase the price by 30-50% because it adds artistic value.

quiz.q: Which steel is best for beginners doing scrollwork?
quiz.explanation: Mild steel is cheap, forgiving, and easy to bend and weld.

quiz.q: What temperature should steel be heated to for bending?
quiz.explanation: Cherry red (about 900Â°C) is the ideal temperature for bending without burning the steel.

quiz.q: What is a scroll jig used for?
options: C) Guiding the bend of a scroll
quiz.explanation: A scroll jig has pins that guide the metal into a consistent spiral shape.

quiz.q: Which tool is essential for making twists?
options: A) A vice and twisting wrench
quiz.explanation: A vice holds one end while a twisting wrench turns the other end to create a twist.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid high-carbon steel for scrolls?
options: B) It cracks when bent cold
quiz.explanation: High-carbon steel is brittle and prone to cracking when bent, especially when cold.

quiz.q: What is the first step in making a scroll?
quiz.explanation: The eye is the small bend at the end of the scroll that starts the spiral.

quiz.q: How many turns are needed for a tight twist on a 300mm bar?
quiz.explanation: Three full turns create a tight, decorative twist.

quiz.q: What should you do if the steel cools while twisting?
quiz.explanation: Cold steel cracks when twisted, so reheating is necessary.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when welding scrolls?
options: B) Not cleaning the metal first
quiz.explanation: Dirt and scale weaken welds; clean metal to bare shine before welding.

quiz.q: How can you prevent rust on finished ironwork?
quiz.explanation: Applying oil or paint while the metal is warm helps it absorb and protect against rust.

quiz.q: What is a good test for mild steel?
options: A) Hit it with a hammer
C) Heat it until it sparks
D) Drop it from a height
quiz.explanation: Mild steel bends without cracking when cold, unlike high-carbon steel.

quiz.q: Why is ventilation important when using a charcoal forge?
options: A) To keep the fire cool
B) To avoid carbon monoxide poisoning
C) To make the steel hotter
quiz.explanation: Charcoal forges produce carbon monoxide, which is deadly in enclosed spaces.

quiz.q: What safety gear is essential when hammering hot metal?
quiz.explanation: Safety glasses protect eyes from flying scale, and gloves protect hands from burns.

quiz.q: What should you do before using a grinder?
options: C) Use it without a handle
quiz.explanation: Loose clothing can get caught in the grinder, causing serious injury.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a fire extinguisher in the workshop?
options: B) To put out fires quickly
quiz.explanation: A fire extinguisher is essential for extinguishing accidental fires before they spread.

quiz.q: How can you make your scrolls more consistent?
options: A) Use a jig and count hammer blows
quiz.explanation: A jig ensures the same shape, and counting blows helps maintain rhythm and consistency.

quiz.q: What is forge welding?
options: B) Welding by hammering hot metal together
quiz.explanation: Forge welding joins metal by heating it to welding heat and hammering the pieces together.

quiz.q: What is the recommended current for welding 10mm mild steel?
quiz.explanation: 80-100 amps is suitable for 2.5mm electrodes on 10mm mild steel.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid synthetic clothing in a forge?
options: B) It melts and sticks to skin
quiz.explanation: Synthetic fabrics melt when exposed to heat, causing severe burns.

quiz.q: What is the final step in the practical exercise?
quiz.explanation: Finishing with oil or paint and then evaluating the work completes the project.

quiz.q: How long should a beginner take to make the practice panel?
quiz.explanation: With practice, the panel should take about 3 hours; aim to reduce to 2 hours.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of uneven twists?
quiz.explanation: If one part of the bar is cooler, it twists less, resulting in an uneven twist.

quiz.q: What should you do if you hear a crack while twisting?
quiz.explanation: A crack means the steel is too cold; stop immediately and reheat to avoid breakage.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store gas cylinders?
options: A) Lying down in the workshop
quiz.explanation: Gas cylinders should be stored upright, outside, to prevent leaks and accidents.

quiz.q: Why is it important to draw full-size templates?
options: B) To plan and avoid mistakes
quiz.explanation: Full-size templates help you visualize and measure accurately before cutting and bending.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of quenching in oil?
options: A) To cool quickly and harden
quiz.explanation: Quenching in oil cools the metal rapidly, but for mild steel it mainly sets the shape and removes scale.

quiz.q: What should you do if you feel dizzy while working?
quiz.explanation: Dizziness can be a sign of heat exhaustion; stop, hydrate, and rest in a cool place.

quiz.q: What is a good way to test if your welds are strong?
options: A) Hit them with a hammer
quiz.explanation: A light hammer tap can reveal weak welds that might break under load.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep a notebook of your work?
options: B) To track mistakes and improvements
C) To use as a template
quiz.explanation: Recording what works and what doesn't helps you improve and avoid repeating mistakes.
